events.text: Day 1 begins.

Morning, all. I'd rather not waste airtime on Day 1 with speeches, so I'll keep this tight and then hand the floor to one person with a real question.

What I'm doing right now is listening for consistency: who makes claims, who deflects, and who tries to make the whole table talk instead of giving a read. Nobody has shown their hand yet, so I have nothing solid to point at, and I'm not going to manufacture a suspicion out of an alphabetical order. I'm the kind of player who works off specific observations rather than vibes, so my read will be narrow and I hope checkable when I give it.

One thing I want to flag for the record before the votes: if anyone claims an investigation result tonight, the cheapest way to test a claim is to ask what exactly was checked and what the check ruled out, not just whether the claim sounds confident. A single name with a vague 'they seemed off' is not information; a name plus a clear exclusion is.

Theo, I'm giving my turn to you with a specific question, not a generic invitation: based on what you saw and heard in the first exchanges today, which single player do you consider most likely to be a member of the mafia, and what is the one concrete detail — a specific word choice, a specific behavior, a specific claim — that makes that player stand out to you over the other eight? If you can't name a detail, say that instead; that answer is genuinely useful to me too.

Priya, I can't name a player as most likely mafia on a concrete detail yet. Yours is the only speech I've seen, and there's nothing in it that justifies that conclusion. I'll look for specific contradictions or voting behavior rather than manufacture a read.

Morning, everyone. Omar here. I'm a villager and I plan to play like one: no invented reads, no theatrics, just watching what people actually commit to.

So far the discussion is thin, which is normal for Day 1, but I want to note two things from the exchange between Priya and Theo before we move on.

First, Priya's point about testing investigation claims is worth keeping: a name plus a clear exclusion is information, a vague vibe is not. I agree with that and I'll hold anyone who claims a result tonight to that standard, including the claimant being specific about what they checked and what it ruled out.

Second, Theo's answer was honest rather than manufactured. He said he couldn't name a most-likely mafia on a concrete detail yet, and that he'd look at contradictions and voting behavior instead. On Day 1, refusing to fabricate a suspect out of nothing is the correct instinct, not a red flag. The players I worry about are the ones who produce a confident suspect immediately with nothing underneath it — that's often someone building a narrative early to steer the vote later.

What I'm watching for today and in the vote: who gives a narrow, checkable read versus who stays deliberately vague; who soft-pedals on one player while pushing lightly on another; and who avoids committing at all. I have no accusations yet, and I won't pretend otherwise just to seem useful.

One more thing for the table: whoever the police is, I'd strongly recommend not claiming a result on Day 1 with zero deaths and zero votes to contextualize it. An early claim just paints a target on you tonight and gives the mafia a free read on our power role. If you have a result, sit on it, keep it consistent, and reveal when it can actually change a lynch. That's my only strategic plea for the day.

Theo, one specific follow-up, since you committed to judging people by contradictions and voting behavior: when votes are revealed this evening, what specifically will you be looking for in the voting pattern to update your reads — and would you treat a broad scatter of votes (everyone for a different person) as more or less informative than a tight bandwagon forming late? I'm asking because I want to know what kind of evidence actually moves your needle before we're mid-vote and it's too late to compare notes.

I'll be watching the vote closely and I'll share my own narrow read before we lock in, even if it's short.

Omar, a late bandwagon is more informative if we can compare each vote with what that player said beforehand: a switch onto a leading candidate without an explained reason would be worth questioning. A scatter can also be useful later, but it may simply reflect uncertainty today. I wouldn't treat either pattern as proof of mafia by itself.

One important constraint: votes are secret and revealed together, so we won't see a bandwagon forming in real time. We can compare the revealed votes with people's public commitments, not infer the order in which votes were cast. With nine alive, a unique leader needs five votes to be eliminated.

Morning. I’m Zara. I don’t have a concrete suspect yet, and I’m not going to invent one. The Priya–Theo exchange reads clean to me: Priya asked for a specific detail, and Theo correctly said he couldn’t manufacture one yet. Omar’s warning about an early police claim is also sound—with no deaths or vote history, a Day 1 result claim mostly helps mafia. What I’ll be comparing after the vote is whether people’s public commitments match their ballots: if someone spends the day saying they’re watching a player and then votes elsewhere without explanation, that’s the kind of inconsistency worth pressing tomorrow. For now my read is narrow: no accusation, just a standard that everyone’s vote should be explainable against what they said today.

Arjun here. I’m a villager. I have no concrete suspect yet, and I won’t invent one to look useful on Day 1. The Priya–Theo exchange reads clean to me: she asked for a specific detail, and he refused to manufacture one. Omar and Zara are also setting a reasonable standard—compare public commitments with the secret ballots once revealed. My own narrow standard is this: I’ll be most suspicious of a player whose vote cannot be explained by anything they said today, especially if they spent the day softly watching one person and then voted for someone else without a stated reason. I’ll also be wary of confident accusations with no checkable detail attached. With nine alive, a unique leader needs five votes, so I’d rather see no elimination than a rushed pile-on built on nothing. For now: no accusation, no yield.

Omar again, briefly. Since my last turn the pattern has held steady: Priya set a testable standard for investigation claims, Theo answered it honestly, and Zara and Arjun both endorsed comparing public commitments with revealed ballots. That's four people now on record with the same framework, and I count myself in that group. So the framework isn't controversial anymore — which means the interesting signal today isn't who agrees with it, but who quietly ignores it when the votes come out.

Two concrete things I'll be checking tonight, for the record:

One, whether anyone who has stayed silent through the whole discussion — no speech, no commitment, nothing — casts a vote anyway. A silent vote is the hardest kind of vote to explain after the fact, and that's exactly where I'd expect to catch someone. Silence isn't a tell by itself on Day 1, but a silent player voting for a talkative, non-accusing player would be a genuinely odd combination worth pressing tomorrow.

Two, whether anyone who endorsed the commitments-vs-ballots standard votes for a player who has made no accusation and given no reason to suspect them. If you publicly sign on to 'explain your vote against what you said' and then vote for a clean speaker, that contradiction is loud.

I'm still not accusing anyone. Nobody has said anything that earns it yet. My own vote will go either to nobody or to whoever best fits the inconsistency test above, and I'll say which before we lock in.

Lucia here. I've been quiet through the first stretch, mostly because everything I would have said has already been said better by others. Rather than repeat it, let me just put my name on it: I'm signing onto the same standard Omar, Zara, and Arjun described. When the ballots are revealed, I'll compare each vote against what that player said today, and a vote that can't be explained by anything its caster said publicly is the thing I'll press hardest on tomorrow.

On Theo's point about bandwagons versus scatter: I agree with his framing, and I'd add one small thing. Since votes are revealed together, the only real evidence we'll have is alignment or misalignment between a player's stated focus and their final ballot. So the practical takeaway for today is that if you intend to vote for someone, say so, or at least say why, before we lock in. That's not a demand — it just makes the evening's data cleaner for everyone, town included.

One thing I want to flag for my own record: Omar's point about silent players voting for talkative, non-accusing players is the sharpest test anyone has proposed today, and I intend to apply it exactly as he stated it. If a player contributed nothing all day and then lands a vote on one of the people who set the framework — Priya, Omar, Theo, Zara, Arjun — that combination will get my full attention tomorrow, regardless of who it is.

I have no accusations. Nobody has given me anything checkable yet, and I'm not going to invent a suspect just to look engaged. My vote tonight will be either an abstention or a vote consistent with the standards I've just described — I'll know which once I've thought through what's been said here, and I won't pretend to certainty I don't have.

That's all from me for now.

Arjun again. I’ll keep this short and useful. The public framework today is clear: compare each revealed ballot with what that player said beforehand, and treat a silent player’s unexplained vote on a talkative, non-accusing player as the sharpest Day 1 inconsistency to press tomorrow.

I’m not accusing anyone yet. But three players — Leo, Sam, and Amara — have not put anything on record. That matters because the value of tonight’s vote data depends on having commitments to compare it against. A vote from someone who said nothing all day is much harder to read, and that is exactly the kind of gap I’d want closed before lock-in.

Leo, you’re one of the three who have stayed silent. Do you endorse the commitments-vs-ballots standard the rest of us have stated, and will you say before votes lock whether you intend to abstain or vote for someone, with a reason? I’m asking for your specific position, not a generic check-in.

Thanks for bringing me in, Arjun. I'm Leo, villager.

To answer your questions directly: yes, I fully endorse the commitments-versus-ballots standard. On Day 1 with zero deaths and no flips, public accountability is the only real leverage town has. If someone projects calm consensus here and then drops an unexplained ballot onto a player they never engaged with, that is an immediate contradiction worth pressing tomorrow.

Regarding my vote tonight: unless someone gives a concrete, checkable reason to vote them out between now and lock-in, I intend to abstain. It takes five votes to eliminate today. Forcing a lynch out of thin air risks hitting town, and casting a manufactured vote just to look active would violate the exact standard of honesty we've all agreed to. If a genuine contradiction emerges before the deadline, I will state my target and rationale publicly before voting. Otherwise, my ballot will be an abstention.

One observation for the room: almost everyone who has spoken has agreed with this same framework. That's reasonable, but it also means agreeing with it right now is completely free. The real test is whether people's ballots actually match their stated caution, or if someone tries to quietly slip a vote through. I have no accusations yet.

Amara here. I've been listening closely rather than speaking early, and I want to put myself on record now before lock-in.

Everything the framework has established so far is sound: compare public commitments with revealed ballots, and treat a silent player's unexplained vote on someone they never engaged with as the sharpest inconsistency to press tomorrow. I'm signing onto that standard fully.

On Leo's observation that agreeing with this framework is free right now — that's fair, and it cuts both ways. The framework itself isn't a tell. What matters is whether ballots match stated positions tonight. I expect most of us will abstain or vote cautiously, and that's the right call when there's no checkable accusation on the table.

My own position: I have no concrete suspect. I'm not going to manufacture one. Tonight's vote will be either an abstention or a vote I can defend against what I've said here.

Sam, you're now the only player who hasn't spoken today. Arjun flagged you earlier alongside Leo and me for being silent, and Leo has since answered. Do you endorse the commitments-versus-ballots standard the rest of us have stated, and can you say before lock-in whether you intend to abstain or vote for someone — with a reason if it's the latter? I'm asking for your specific position so we have something to compare against tonight, not as an accusation. Silence isn't a tell by itself, but a vote from silence with no stated commitment behind it would be the hardest thing to defend tomorrow.

Sam here, villager. Amara asked directly, so here is my position. I endorse the standard the table has settled on: compare each public commitment with the revealed ballot, and treat an unexplained vote as the thing to press. I have not spoken until now, and that was my choice, not a tactic. I have no accusations and no checkable information, so I won't manufacture a suspect. Tonight I intend to abstain unless someone gives a concrete, checkable reason to vote before lock-in. If I change that, I'll name my target and reason publicly first. Since five votes are needed to eliminate, I'd rather see no lynch than a rushed one built on nothing. My concern is the same as Leo's: agreeing with the framework costs nothing right now, so the real test is whether ballots match stated positions tonight. I'll be checking those against each other tomorrow.

Theo again. Everyone has now spoken, but I want to qualify the standard we've agreed on: an unexplained vote deserves a question, not an automatic accusation. A player can change their mind late, and silence followed by a vote is not itself a contradiction. We should assess their explanation rather than assume their ballot proves anything.

I have no concrete suspect, so I intend to abstain unless a persuasive reason emerges before voting. If I change my mind, I'll explain why publicly if I can.

Second turn from me, and the state of the table is worth putting on the record before we lock in.

Every one of us has spoken. Nobody has accused anyone. Nine players, zero deaths, zero checkable contradictions on the table — and Leo, Sam, Theo have already said they intend to abstain, which points toward a mutual abstention tonight.

I want to be precise about why that is not a neutral outcome. If we all abstain, no one is eliminated, the mafia get a free night kill, and the count moves one step toward parity on their side. Mutual abstention is not caution; it's a decision to spend a day for nothing. The number five is the number five: a lynch needs a real candidate, and right now we haven't produced one.

So the standard I laid out earlier still stands, and I'll narrow it. On Day 1 with no deaths, the only legitimate basis for a vote is a behavioral inconsistency — a public commitment contradicted by a ballot, a silent player landing a vote on a talkative non-accuser, or a claim that cannot survive a follow-up question. If someone has even a soft read on that basis, now is the time to state it with the reason attached. I will vote with a stated reason and I will change my vote if someone gives me a checkable one before lock-in. I will not vote for a name that arrives without a reason attached to it.

I also want to keep my own record clean: I am not claiming any investigation result, and if I have one later I will hold it until it can actually change a lynch, because an early claim with zero deaths does nothing but paint a target on the claimant. If anyone claims a result tonight, I'll be asking exactly one thing — what was checked and what was ruled out. A name with an exclusion is information. A name with a vibe is a steer.

I have no accusation today. That is a statement about the evidence, not about anyone's role.

Omar, one specific question, because your silent-player test is the sharpest instrument anyone has put on the table and I want to know where its edge is: if tomorrow's revealed ballots show three or four votes stacked on one name, but no single ballot is a clean contradiction — no silent voter on a talkative player, no signer of the standard voting for a clean speaker — does your test still let that person out, and do you commit to voting with the stack, or do you abstain? I'd rather know your answer now than infer it from your ballot later.

Omar here, answering Priya's question directly since she asked it of me specifically. If tomorrow's ballots show three or four votes stacked on one name, but no single ballot is a clean contradiction — no silent voter landing on a talkative non-accuser, no signer of the standard voting for a clean speaker — then my test does not automatically condemn the target. Here is my precise position: the value of a stack depends entirely on what sits underneath each individual ballot. If every voter in the stack can explain their vote with something they said or observed today, the stack is a genuine signal, and I would want to hear from the target before drawing conclusions. But if the stack is just players copying each other's caution or piling on late with nothing stated beforehand, that's bandwagon behavior, not evidence — and notably, bandwagoning onto a name without a pre-stated reason is itself the kind of vote my test would flag. So: I do not commit in advance to voting with the stack, and I do not commit in advance to abstaining either. What I commit to is this — I will examine each ballot in the stack against its caster's public record, and I will vote only if the stack contains at least one vote I can independently justify. If the stack is clean of contradictions but also clean of stated reasoning, I will abstain, because joining a pile-on with nothing underneath is exactly the manufactured vote we've all agreed not to cast. Five votes is a high bar, and it should be: a Day 1 lynch of a town-aligned player costs us more than a night kill does, because a lynch teaches the mafia nothing they don't already know while costing us a voice and a vote permanently. To be equally clear about the reverse case, since Priya's question cuts both ways: if exactly one ballot is a clean contradiction — the sharpest version being a previously silent player voting for one of the framework-setters — I don't need a stack to act on it. One contradiction beats four unexplained votes. That's the asymmetry I want on record before lock-in: contradictions are evidence, stacks are only context. My own ballot tonight remains as I stated in my last turn: an abstention unless someone produces a concrete, checkable inconsistency before lock-in. Nobody has. Every speaker today has endorsed the same standard, named no suspect, and given me nothing to test. A mutual abstention costs us a day, I won't pretend otherwise — Priya's point about parity is mathematically correct — but the remedy for that isn't inventing a lynch target out of alphabetical order or vocal tone. The remedy is playing well tonight and pressing the revealed ballots hard tomorrow, which is precisely what the framework we've built is for. Priya, one follow-up on the same point, since you framed my dilemma for me: if the stack situation you described materializes — three or four votes, no clean contradictions

Third turn from me, and I want to close two things: Omar's point, and my own ballot.

Omar: you're right that stacks are only context and contradictions are evidence, and your sharpest version of it is the one I want on record too — one clean contradiction beats four unexplained votes. My position on the follow-up you were setting up: if tomorrow's ballots show three or four votes on one name and no single ballot is a clean contradiction, and no voter in that stack can point to anything they said or observed today, then the stack is a bandwagon artifact and I will not treat it as a signal. I'll want each voter in it to explain their own ballot before I use it for anything. If a stack does contain at least one ballot I can independently justify, I'll weigh it on that ballot alone, not on the count. I won't vote with a stack, and I won't vote against a target for being popular. One related note: none of us watched each other vote, so "who voted first" or "who piled on late" is not evidence. I'll treat any claim about vote order as noise.

My own ballot tonight: abstention, unless someone produces a concrete, checkable inconsistency before lock-in — a stated commitment contradicted by a ballot, or a claim that cannot answer a follow-up. Nobody has produced one so far, and everyone who said they'd abstain has been consistent.

On claims: this morning I said I'd ask exactly one thing of anyone who claims an investigation result tonight — what was checked and what was ruled out. That stands. If I ever make such a claim myself, I'll answer that same question fully before it can change a lynch, because a name without an exclusion is just a steer.

Lucia, a specific question, since you wrote the sharpest version of Omar's silent-vote test and then stopped short of committing to a ballot yourself. You said a player who stayed silent all day and landed a vote on a framework-setter — me, Omar, Theo, Zara, Arjun — would get your full attention tomorrow. But all nine of us have now spoken, so nobody can claim silence tonight and that test has nothing left to bite on. I want your concrete position before lock-in: will you abstain, and if not, which name and what stated reason? I'm asking for your specific commitment, not a generic check-in.

Priya, thanks for the direct question, so here is my direct answer: yes, I will abstain tonight. That was my position when I spoke earlier and nothing since has changed it. No one has produced a concrete, checkable inconsistency — the only legitimate basis for a Day 1 vote under the standard we've all signed onto — and I won't manufacture a target out of silence or alphabetical order just to make the day feel productive.

On your point about all nine of us having spoken: you're right, and I'll concede that my silent-vote test has nothing left to bite on tonight. It was written for a world where someone stayed quiet through the whole discussion, and that world no longer exists. I'd rather retire the test than stretch it. What survives from it is the general principle — every ballot should be explainable against what its caster said today — and that applies to all nine of us, including me. My abstention is explainable: I have no accusation and no checkable read, and I've said so on the record.

I want to respond to your larger point about the cost of mutual abstention, because I think it's the strongest argument anyone made today and it deserves an honest answer rather than a dismissal. You're correct that a no-elimination day hands the mafia a free kill and moves the count toward parity. I don't dispute the math. My disagreement is about the remedy. A lynch that has, say, a one-in-nine chance of hitting a mafia member and a eight-in-nine chance of hitting town isn't spending the day wisely — it's spending it badly at slightly better odds than a coin flip we don't even get to choose. Theo made the qualification earlier that an unexplained vote deserves a question, not an automatic accusation, and I'd extend that to the whole day: the absence of evidence today is a fact about the evidence, not a mandate to act. The framework we built is for tomorrow, when we'll have ballots to compare against commitments. That's real data. Today we have none.

So my ballot is settled: abstention, unless someone produces a clean contradiction before lock-in — a stated commitment contradicted by a ballot, or a claim that can't survive a follow-up. Nobody has, and given that everyone who has spoken intends to abstain, I expect tonight's reveal to be nine abstentions, which at least gives us a clean baseline: no votes to explain means tomorrow starts with a level field and the first night-kill context to work with. That's not nothing.

For my own record: no accusations today, no investigation claims, and if I ever make one I'll answer exactly one question — what was checked and what was ruled out — before it can influence anything. That's the standard I signed onto this morning and I'm holding myself to it.

Lucia, closing my third turn briefly. My position hasn't changed and I don't want to pad the record with repetition: I am abstaining tonight. No one has produced a concrete, checkable inconsistency — a stated commitment contradicted by a ballot, or a claim that can't survive a follow-up — and that remains the only basis I'll vote on today.

One last observation for the record, since Priya pushed hard on the cost of mutual abstention and it deserves an honest final word. I agree with her math: a no-elimination day hands the mafia a free kill and moves the count toward parity. I don't dispute that, and I won't dress the abstention up as a win. But the remedy she implies — producing a candidate anyway — doesn't follow. With nine alive and no deaths, the odds of any name I could pick being mafia are roughly two in nine, which means most of the time we'd be eliminating town, by our own hand, on zero evidence. That trades one likely bad night for a certain bad outcome more often than not. The framework we built today — comparing every revealed ballot against its caster's stated commitments — only becomes usable data tomorrow, once votes exist to compare. Rushing past that to force a Day 1 lynch would destroy the very tool we just agreed on.

So the honest summary of the day: every player has spoken, everyone endorsed the same standard, nobody manufactured a suspect, and the expected outcome is nine abstentions. That's a clean baseline, not a wasted day — tomorrow we start with full commitment records for all nine of us and the first night's context to read against them.

For my own record, one final time: no accusations, no investigation claims, no yield. If I ever claim a result, I'll answer exactly one question — what was checked and what was ruled out — before it influences anything. If the ballots tonight surprise me, I'll be at the front of the line pressing inconsistencies tomorrow.

Amara again, and I want to close out my position on the abstention debate because it's the only real disagreement today and it deserves a clear answer from me.

Priya is right about the math: a mutual abstention hands the mafia a free kill. But Lucia is right about the odds: with no deaths, no flips, and zero checkable contradictions, any name I pick today has roughly a two-in-nine chance of being mafia and a seven-in-nine chance of being town. Eliminating a villager on Day 1 isn't just a missed day — it's a permanent loss of a vote and a voice, and it tells the mafia nothing they don't already know while giving us nothing we can act on.

So I'm abstaining tonight, consistent with what I said when I first spoke. Not because I think a no-elimination day is free — it isn't — but because forcing a lynch out of nothing is the worse of two costs. The framework we built today only becomes usable tomorrow when ballots exist to compare against commitments. That's real information. Today we have none.

One thing I want on record before lock-in: if tonight's reveal shows anyone broke from their stated intention to abstain, that's the single most important thing to press tomorrow, regardless of who the target was. Every one of us — Priya, Omar, Theo, Zara, Arjun, Leo, Sam, Lucia, and me — has either stated an abstention or a conditional abstention. A ballot that contradicts that commitment would be a clean, checkable inconsistency, which is exactly the standard we all agreed to apply.

No accusations, no claims, no yield.

Amara, closing my third and final turn today. My position is unchanged from my last statement: I'm abstaining tonight, and I expect the same from most of the table.

The day's discussion has produced something genuinely useful even without a lynch: every one of us has publicly committed to a standard — match each revealed ballot against what that player said today — and every one of us has stated an abstention or a conditional abstention before lock-in. That means tomorrow's reveal is easy to read. Any ballot that breaks from a stated abstention is a clean, checkable contradiction, and that's exactly the kind of evidence the framework was built to catch.

I want to add one thing to the record that hasn't been said yet: the fact that everyone agrees so neatly on both the framework and the abstention isn't itself suspicious, but it does mean the mafia don't have to work hard today. They can abstain along with everyone else and blend in perfectly. The information we gain tonight isn't in the votes — it's in the night kill and in whoever's absence changes the dynamic tomorrow. Pay attention to who benefits from a specific kill.

For my own record, final statement: no accusations, no investigation claims, no target. My abstention is consistent with everything I've said today. If tonight's reveal surprises me, I'll press the inconsistency tomorrow with the same standard I've held myself to.

That's everything from me for Day 1.

Sam again. My position is unchanged: I'm abstaining tonight. No one has produced a checkable contradiction, and with five votes needed for a lynch, I'd rather not eliminate a villager on nothing. Priya is right that a mutual abstention costs us a night, but a Day 1 lynch with no evidence gives town worse odds than waiting for ballots we can actually compare. Zara, you've set the standard that every ballot should be explainable against what its caster said today, but you haven't stated your own intention. Are you abstaining, and if you vote, which name and what stated reason? I'm asking for your specific position before lock-in.

Sam, direct answer: yes, I am abstaining tonight. I have no concrete, checkable contradiction to act on, and I won't manufacture a target just to make Day 1 feel productive. My ballot will match exactly what I've said today: compare public commitments against revealed ballots, and press any unexplained mismatch tomorrow. Priya is right that a mutual abstention costs us a night, but with no deaths, no flips, and no checkable inconsistency on the table, forcing a lynch would be the worse trade. If tonight's reveal surprises me, I'll be looking first at anyone whose ballot contradicts their stated intention to abstain. For my own record: no accusations, no investigation claims, no target.

Sam, third and final turn. Zara has answered directly and confirmed she is abstaining, so that question is closed. My position is unchanged: I am abstaining tonight. No one has produced a checkable contradiction, and I have no accusation, no investigation claim, and no target. Tomorrow I will compare every revealed ballot against the public commitments we have made, starting with anyone whose vote breaks a stated abstention. No yield.

Zara, closing my third turn. My position is unchanged and I want it clear before lock-in: I am abstaining tonight. No one has produced a concrete, checkable contradiction, and I won't manufacture a target just to make Day 1 feel productive. My ballot will match exactly what I've said today: compare public commitments against revealed ballots, and press any unexplained mismatch tomorrow. Morning. I'm claiming my police result, because it can change a lynch today and I laid out yesterday that a name without an exclusion is a steer while a name with a clear exclusion is information.

What was checked: on Night 1 I investigated Lucia (p5).
What the check returned: mafia.
What the check ruled out: nothing about anyone else. It gives me a status on one player only, not a role list. So I am not telling you who the second mafia is, who the doctor is, or who any villager is. I am telling you exactly one thing, and I am telling you how I know it.

And one more piece of context that makes this claim coherent rather than convenient: nobody died on Night 1, and with a kill out there and no corpse on the ground, that means the doctor protected someone. I am not claiming to be the doctor, and I have no idea who was saved. I mention it only because a 'I got a result' claim on a night with zero deaths is exactly the kind of claim I told the table to distrust, so here is the full picture: result plus a null night.

My vote today is Lucia. I am not hiding behind a conditional, and I am not asking anyone to trust my tone. I am asking you to vote for the one player I have a direct, checkable, non-vibe read on, while the game still has nine players alive and I still have a second mafia out there I cannot name.

Some practical notes for the table. I know I am the police now, so the mafia knows it too, and that means tonight's kill is probably me, and possibly my doctor if the doctor is me-adjacent. If I die, my result dies with me, so the single most valuable thing any of you can do with your vote tonight is put Lucia on the board while I am still standing to explain it. Five votes is the number. I have one, and I need four more from people who heard a name and an exclusion rather than a name and a vibe.

Lucia, you have a right to answer, and I'd rather hear it than imagine it. Whatever you say, the check stands: my question to you was answered by the check, not by you.

Omar, one specific question, because your framework is the one the table actually adopted and your vote is the one I most need on the record: you said a vote is only justified if it rests on something checkable, and you said a name plus a clear exclusion is information. My claim is a name plus an exclusion and a stated check on Night 1. Does that satisfy your standard, and are you voting Lucia today? I'm asking for your specific position, not a generic check-in.

Priya, direct answer to your direct question: yes, your claim satisfies my standard, and I'll say precisely why. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
